$comment: Home-page demo: a real consultation, run on the live site (bigjospaints.vercel.app/colour-consultant) on 11 Oct 2026 with OpenAI GPT-5.5. The photo is a real living room photographed by Patrick Perkins on Unsplash (src/assets/photos/apartment.jpg; credit in src/lib/photos.ts), sent at 1600 px as the consultant's own upload does. The brief is as sent. roomRead, title, why and tip are the AI's words, unedited; litres and prices are worked out from catalogue.json when the site is built, exactly as the consultant does. public/demo/walls.png marks the white walls (white = wall) for the tinted preview: the wall areas are drawn by hand, because the shelves, blinds and window are white too, and inside them a pixel counts as wall by its colour (CIELAB lightness, chroma, hue).
brief: Our lounge is all plain white and feels a bit flat. We'd like some colour that still keeps it light and calm, with all our plants and the wooden floor.
roomRead: The lounge is compact but bright, with warm wooden floors, a grey sofa, white built-ins and plenty of green plants, so a light nature-led colour will add depth without closing it in.

options.title: Soft garden calm
options.why: This pale grey-green will gently pick up the plants and soften the plain white walls. It stays light enough for all four walls in your 4 × 4 m lounge.
options.tip: Keep the ceiling and trim a clean warm white so the room still feels fresh.

options.title: Warm and natural
options.why: The sandy beige tone works beautifully with the wooden floor and timber furniture. It will make the lounge feel warmer while still calm and airy.
options.tip: Pair it with white shelves and a few green or terracotta plant pots for an easy layered look.

options.title: Fresh leafy feel
options.why: This soft sage is a little more colourful, but still muted enough for a relaxed lounge. It links the walls to your plants and sits nicely against the grey sofa.
options.tip: Use warm wood, cream textiles and black accents to keep the sage looking grown-up rather than too sweet.
